pedagogy.summary: Children learn to read and use the £ and p symbols and to combine coins to make a stated amount. The language work is: saying and writing amounts correctly ('fifty pence' = 50p; 'one pound fifty'), reading prices, and — the key notation rule — NOT writing £ and p together (£1.50p is wrong; write 150p, or £1 and 50p, or £1.50). At Year 2 pounds and pence are recorded separately, and the same amount has more than one correct written form (150p is the same money as £1 and 50p). Taught by using money language in real shop / price contexts and listening for correct USE.
bestPractices: Use £ and p in real contexts — price tags, shopping role-play — and listen for correct use
Read amounts aloud both ways (150p / one pound fifty) and match them to written prices
Teach the notation rule explicitly: never write £ and p together (not £1.50p)
Combine coins to hit a target amount, saying the running total by value
Record pounds and pence separately at Year 2
keyRepresentations: Price tags and till displays showing £ and p
Real coins combined to make a target amount
A 'say it / write it' pairing (150p to £1 and 50p)
A part-whole model of an amount split into coins
commonMisconceptions: Muddles the two symbols or which side the symbol goes
Reads 150p and £1 and 50p as different amounts (misses the equivalence)
When combining coins, counts the number of coins rather than their value toward the total

learn.summary: Year 2 children recognise and use the £ and p symbols, read and say amounts of money two ways (150p and 'one pound and fifty pence'), and combine coins to make a stated target amount by tracking value. The central notation rule is that £ and p are never written together: '£1.50p' is wrong — write 150p, or £1 and 50p, or £1.50. At Year 2 pounds and pence are recorded separately and the same amount has more than one correct written form (150p is the same money as £1 and 50p). Taught through real shop/price contexts, listening for correct use rather than asking for symbol definitions.

activities.title: Build a price with coins and record it correctly
feedback: If a child writes '£1.50p' or '£50p', stop at the point of writing: 'We never write the pound sign and the p together.' Then help them rewrite the amount they actually meant: for one pound and fifty pence write £1.50, 150p or £1 and 50p; for fifty pence write 50p.

If a child says 'I've got three coins, so that's enough' regardless of value, re-count the VALUE onto the total as each coin lands ('50... 70... 75') and ask whether the total — not the count — matches the price.

If a child treats 150p and '£1 and 50p' as different amounts, lay the two forms beside the same coins and count their value: 100p makes one pound, and 50p more makes 150p, which is one pound and fifty pence.
activities.rationale: The National Curriculum requires Year 2 pupils to use the £ and p symbols and combine amounts to make a particular value; building to a target with coins while recording makes the notation rule live at the point of writing. An optional interactive version — dragging coins into a till where the display writes the running total in correct notation, rejects '£1.50p', and offers a 'say it two ways' toggle flipping 150p to '£1 and 50p' — may make the feedback immediate; this is one proposed way to realise the task, not a requirement.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils should 'recognise and use symbols for pounds (£) and pence (p); combine amounts to make a particular value'.

NCETM guidance states the writing convention explicitly: 'It is important that children do not write the £ and p together: 100p, £1.00, but not £1.00p', and that pupils 'read and say amounts of money confidently and use the symbols £ and p accurately, recording pounds and pence separately'.
learnerActions: Look at a price tag (e.g. 75p, or £1 and 50p) and choose real or on-screen coins to make exactly that amount
Say the running total by VALUE as each coin is added — e.g. '50... 70... 75' — not by the number of coins
Write the amount down in a correct form, then write it a second way if possible (150p / £1 and 50p)
Check your written amount against the rule: never put £ and p together
activities.intendedInsight: An amount of money can be built from coins by adding their values to a target, and the same amount has more than one correct written form, but £ and p are never written together.

activities.title: Shop role-play: pay, read tags and spot a wrong price
feedback: If the child reads '£1.50p' happily without noticing a problem, prompt: 'Someone wrote the pound sign AND the p — can we do that? How should it be written instead?'
If the child pays with the wrong value, re-say the price and count the value of the coins handed over together.
Praise reading an amount both ways (150p and 'one pound and fifty pence') as a sign of understanding equivalence.
activities.rationale: Because the objective is USING money language in authentic context, a spoken shop exchange elicits real use — reading tags, paying, and judging notation — rather than defining symbols in the abstract. A conversational character naming prices and asking the child to pay and read is one proposed format; a sort or matching item alone would check recognition but would not elicit this spoken use.

learnerActions: Take part in a shop/market-stall exchange where a shopkeeper names a price ('one pound and fifty pence') and asks you to make and hand over that amount in coins
Read a price tag aloud (e.g. read '150p' and offer an equivalent spoken form)
Judge a price written as '£1.50p': say whether it looks right and explain what is wrong with it
activities.intendedInsight: Money language is used in context — reading, saying and paying amounts — and a confident user flags '£1.50p' as wrongly written because £ and p should not appear together.

activities.title: Match and write amounts; catch the notation error
feedback: For a matching error, place the same coins beside both forms so the equivalence is visible.
For an accepted '£1.50p', state the rule and ask for a correct rewrite (£1.50 / 150p / £1 and 50p).
For a combine-to-target error, recount by value, not by number of coins.
activities.rationale: Short written and matching items let the child practise producing correct notation and identifying the £/p error. These recognition and short-answer items check and rehearse the rule; they do not by themselves demonstrate confident use in a real context, so pair them with the building and role-play activities above.

NCETM guidance states the writing convention explicitly: 'It is important that children do not write the £ and p together: 100p, £1.00, but not £1.00p', and that pupils 'read and say amounts of money confidently and use the symbols £ and p accurately, recording pounds and pence separately'.
learnerActions: Write a given price (e.g. hear '75p' spoken, write the amount) using correct notation
Match a spoken or written form to its equivalent: draw a line from '150p' to '£1 and 50p'
Combine coins to reach a stated total such as 75p (e.g. 50p + 20p + 5p)
Decide whether '£1.50p' is written correctly and, if not, rewrite it
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising correct notation and equivalent forms, and selecting coins that sum to a target, consolidate the rule that £ and p are recorded separately.

constraints: At Year 2 the central rule is recording pounds and pence separately and never writing £ and p together. The objective and the verified NCETM convention accept forms such as £1.50 and £1.00 (but not £1.50p); accept £1.50 as correct. The White Rose scheme (verified:false in the row) suggests Year 2 avoids decimal notation and uses 'and' (£5 and 30p); treat that stricter 'no decimal' guidance as unverified and do NOT use it to reject £1.50.
Keep any pence component below 100p when writing the split form (£1 and 50p, not £1 and 150p); this does not forbid the all-pence form 150p, which is a valid written form throughout.
The same amount has more than one correct written form (150p = £1 and 50p = £1.50); accept any correct form and treat them as equal money.
Assess by listening for correct USE in context — avoid asking the child to define a symbol in the abstract, as stated in the source's assessment approach.
A static price-tag poster or tap-to-reveal image can label £ and p but does not let the child build amounts or use the symbols in context; treat it as a labelling scaffold, not the main task.
Recognition/matching items check and rehearse the convention but do not by themselves elicit independent construction or real-context use; combine them with building and speaking tasks.
Interactive feedback examples (till display writing the running total, rejecting '£1.50p', 'say it two ways' toggle) are optional proposed illustrations of the mechanism, not required technology.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original catalog claimed a 3D/spatial format 'adds nothing' and that a static image 'can't' teach use in context. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established findings; softened to narrowly scoped affordance/limit statements. A static image can still teach labelling.

The White Rose Education scheme is marked verified:false in the row; its Year-2 'record pounds and pence separately, pence below 100p, use "and" not decimal' guidance is unverified and conflicts with the objective's listed correct form £1.50, so it is not applied as a hard constraint against £1.50.
The example 150p = £1 and 50p was checked for arithmetic consistency: 150 pence = £1 (100p) + 50p — correct. 75p = 50p + 20p + 5p is correct. '£1.50p' is correctly flagged as invalid notation.

probeDeeper: 'You read 150p — is that the same as £1 and 50p, or different? Show me with the coins.'
'Someone wrote £1.50p — what is wrong with that?'
'As you add each coin, what is the total now?' (value not count)
'Is 5p the same as £5? How would you write five pounds?' (the symbol and its place matter)
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the price correctly and offers an equivalent form (150p is £1 and 50p); combines coins to make 75p while tracking the value (not the count); recognises '£1.50p' as wrongly written because £ and p should not appear together.

errorPatterns.pattern: Writes or accepts £ and p together (£1.50p, £50p)
errorPatterns.nextMove: State and rehearse the rule in context — pounds and pence are recorded separately (150p, or £1 and 50p, or £1.50), never £ and p together; correct it at the point of writing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes £1.50p, or reads it as fine when asked if it looks right

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads 150p and '£1 and 50p' as different amounts — doesn't hold the equivalence
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pair the two forms with the same coins in front of the child; count 150 pennies as one pound and fifty pence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 150p and £1 and 50p are not the same money

errorPatterns.pattern: When combining coins, tracks the NUMBER of coins rather than their value toward the target
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the VALUE onto the total each time a coin is added ('50... 70... 75'), not the number of coins.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says 'I've got three coins, so that's enough' regardless of the coins' values

responseLevels.gap: Muddles £ and p, writes them together, or treats 150p and £1 and 50p as different; counts coins by number.
responseLevels.full: Reads and writes amounts in correct £/p notation (never £ and p together), holds the 150p to £1 and 50p equivalence, and combines coins to a target by tracking value.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and writes simple amounts and combines coins for easy totals, but slips on the £/p equivalence or writes £ and p together under pressure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a shopping context, listen for correct USE (never ask the child to define a symbol): (1) Show a price written '150p': 'Read this price to me', then 'Can you write it another way?' (2) 'I want to buy something that costs 75p — use these coins to make 75p and tell me the total as you go.' (3) Show '£1.50p' written down: 'Does this look right to you? Read it.' Listen for correct reading, the £/p equivalence, and whether they flag £ and p written together.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The '£1.50p — does this look right?' item is the hinge: a child who has the notation convention flags it, while one who hasn't reads it happily. Making 75p while stating the running total catches counting coins by number rather than value.
